title: Internal-state criticality in Bayesian-inverse-Bayesian inference
abstract: We propose Bayesian-inverse-Bayesian (BIB) inference in repeated games as a minimal generative model linking Bayesian inference, statistical mechanics, and heavy-tailed statistics. As a concrete instantiation we simulate repeated $N$-hand cyclic-dominance rock-paper-scissors, a discrete setting in which Nash-targeting algorithms collapse to uniform random play, so that any non-trivial dynamics must originate internally. Across a multi-axis sweep of design, window, and opponent conditions, the BIB dynamics remain in the same internal critical state, the argmax-persistence distribution staying a heavy-tailed power law with exponent $α\approx 1.43$ at the canonical window. Along the window and alphabet axes the exponent is not constant but drifts toward the universal $3/2$ as the finite-sample residual $(N-1)/(2m)$ vanishes. Bayes-only inference, which lacks the inverse step, shows no analogous universality and no power law. Because the argmax and laminar observables are first-passage reads of one driftless log-posterior walk, what is robust across conditions is the critical, zero-drift state itself, evidenced by the cross-design data collapse rather than by any particular exponent value. The state is also invariant across the hypothesis count $N_h$, with the cutoff time and posterior spread obeying finite-size scaling. Adding an inverse-Bayesian relaxation step (hypothesis renewal) to ordinary Bayesian inference is by itself enough to render the dynamics critical, with no external parameter adjustment. Rather than self-organizing toward an absorbing state, BIB reaches criticality by continually reconstructing the hypothesis-space boundary, a mechanism complementary to self-organized criticality that makes the criticality robust across a natural parameter range.
summary: This paper proposes Bayesian-inverse-Bayesian (BIB) inference as a generative model that naturally generates critical dynamics. By adding an inverse step to standard Bayesian updating, the system achieves a robust internal critical state characterized by heavy-tailed persistence statistics. This mechanism is argued to be fundamentally different from simple adaptive learning or external tuning parameters.
main_problem: To find a minimal generative model where criticality emerges intrinsically from the inference process itself, bridging game theory optimization with observed heavy-tailed decision statistics.
main_result: Bayesian-inverse-Bayesian (BIB) inference maintains an internal critical state characterized by power-law persistence distributions ($\alpha \approx 1.43$) due to a boundary-reconstructing renewal mechanism.
method: The authors simulate the BIB update rule on repeated N-hand cyclic-dominance Rock-Paper-Scissors, comparing it against standard Bayes-only inference (BO).
model_or_system: The model is an adaptive learning process applied to a discrete game (N-hand RPS), where the core mechanism involves augmenting Bayesian updates with an inverse step that replaces low-support hypotheses with empirical observation histograms.
key_observables: $	ext{argmax}$-persistence distribution exponent ($\alpha$), laminar phase length distribution, and posterior spread scaling ($\sigma \propto N^{- eta_h}$).
important_parameters: Window size ($m$), number of hands ($N$), hypothesis count ($N_h$), and the residual drift term $(N-1)/(2m)$.
main_assumptions: The critical state is robustly characterized by the on-off intermittency class, suggesting a zero-drift internal mechanism rather than external tuning.
figures_summary: Figures compare CCDFs of persistence times for BIB vs. BO, showing distinct heavy-tailed behavior; other figures illustrate parameter sweeps confirming robustness and convergence to theoretical exponents like $3/2$.
paper_structure: The paper develops the argument by first defining the BIB mechanism, then analyzing its resulting power-law statistics across multiple axes (N, m, Nh), contrasting it with BO inference, and finally assigning the observed critical behavior to a specific internal renewal process.
why_interesting: While not directly about quantum systems, the concept of 'internal-state criticality' arising from an information processing rule provides a powerful analogy for understanding non-equilibrium dynamics in complex quantum many-body systems or open quantum systems where measurement/feedback drives emergent order.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic of the Bayesian and inverse-Bayesian steps and the resulting internal-state critical dynamics. The Bayesian update (left) contracts the posterior, concentrating mass on data-supporting hypotheses. The inverse-Bayesian replacement (right) renews the hypothesis set, injecting a new hypothesis that reflects the recent empirical pattern. Together, the Bayesian concentration and the inverse-Bayesian renewal give rise to a critical state characterized by a power-law persistence-time distribution P(Targmax) ∼T −α, where Targmax is the number of consecutive steps the posterior’s most-probable hypothesis remains unchanged.

FIG. 2. Hypothesis-space dynamics, BIB-BIB (left column) versus BO-BO (right column). Same random seed, rs design (random init, sample), Nh = 10, m = 50, T = 1500. (a, d) Hand sequence of agent A (R yellow, P blue, S green). (b, e) Posterior P(h) heatmap with the argmax trajectory overlaid (white line). (c, f) Top-3 P(h) trajectories with the uniform reference 1/Nh shown as a dotted line.

FIG. 3. Design-independent collapse of the BIB argmax- persistence exponent and its absence under Bayes-only updat- ing. Argmax-persistence CCDFs, the four BIB-BIB designs (red) collapse onto a single heavy tail (α ≈1.43), whereas BO-BO (blue, random- versus structured-initialization fam- ilies) departs from a power law at the shortest persistence times. T = 2 × 105 × 20 runs, Nh = 10, m = 50.

FIG. 4. Specificity of the critical class to the inverse-Bayesian rule among adaptive learners. Internal argmax-persistence CCDFs of BIB (red circles, shaded band over the four designs rs/ra/ss/sa) versus standard learners at Nh = 10, m = 50, T = 2 × 105 (40 seeds), showing the played-action run length for the reactive baselines Q-learning (blue triangles) and WSLS (green diamonds) and the argmax cumulative regret for regret matching (orange squares). (a) Against a uniform-random opponent. (b) In self-play. Dashed curves are truncated-power-law fits. The dotted guide is the on-off α = 3/2 slope.
